# Authentication

Copy page Copied

All requests to Datadog’s API must be authenticated. Requests that write data require reporting access and require an `API key`. Requests that read data require full access and also require an `application key`.

Note: All Datadog API clients are configured by default to consume Datadog US site APIs. If you are on the Datadog EU site, set the environment variable `DATADOG_HOST` to `https://api.datadoghq.eu` or override this value directly when creating your client.

Manage your account’s API and application keys in Datadog, and see the API and Application Keys page in the documentation.

The API uses resource-oriented URLs to call the API, uses status codes to indicate the success or failure of requests, returns JSON from all requests, and uses standard HTTP response codes. Use the Datadog API to access the Datadog platform programmatically. Getting started Authenticate to the API with an API key using the header DD-API-KEY . For some endpoints, you also need an Application key , which uses the header DD-APPLICATION-KEY . To try out the API Note : To authenticate to the Datadog API through Postman, add your Datadog API and Application key values to the Collection variables of the Datadog API collection. Using the API is a guide to the endpoints. Notes : Add your API and application key values to the Variables tab of the Datadog API Collection. cURL code examples assume usage of BASH and GNU coreutils. On macOS, you can install coreutils with the Homebrew package manager : brew install coreutils Client libraries By default, the Datadog API Docs show examples in cURL. Select one of our official client libraries languages in each endpoint to see code examples from that library. To install each library: Java Python [legacy] Python Ruby [legacy] Ruby Go TypeScript Rust Installation Maven - Add this dependency to your project's POM: Copy <dependency> <groupId> com.datadoghq </groupId> <artifactId> datadog-api-client </artifactId> <version> 2.62.0 </version> <scope> compile </scope> </dependency> Gradle - Add this dependency to your project's build file: Copy compile "com.datadoghq:datadog-api-client:2.62.0" Usage Copy import com.datadog.api.client.ApiClient; import com.datadog.api.client.ApiException; import com.datadog.api.client.Configuration; import com.datadog.api.<VERSION>.client.api.*; import com.datadog.api.<VERSION>.client.model.*; Note : Replace <VERSION> with v1 or v2, depending on which endpoints you want to use. Examples Maven pom.xml for running examples: Copy <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example </groupId> <artifactId> example </artifactId> <version> 1 </version> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.datadoghq </groupId> <artifactId> datadog-api-client </artifactId> <version> 2.62.0 </version> <scope> compile </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> Make sure that CLASSPATH variable contains all dependencies. Copy export CLASSPATH=$(mvn -q exec:exec -Dexec.executable=echo -Dexec.args="%classpath" ) Gradle build.gradle for running examples: Copy plugins { id 'java' id 'application' } repositories { jcenter() } dependencies { implementation 'com.datadoghq:datadog-api-client:2.62.0' } application { mainClassName = 'Example.java' } Execute example by running gradle run command. Installation The package is under @datadog/datadog-api-client and can be installed through NPM or Yarn: Copy # NPM npm install @datadog/datadog-api-client # Yarn yarn add @datadog/datadog-api-client Usage Copy import { <VERSION> } from 'datadog-api-client' ; Note : Replace <VERSION> with v1 or v2, depending on which endpoints you want to use. To build the endpoint for your site, add mcp. before your site parameter and append /v1/mcp . Use the endpoint that matches the site where your Datadog organization is hosted: Site Site parameter MCP Server endpoint US1 datadoghq.com https://mcp.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp US3 us3.datadoghq.com https://mcp.us3.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp US5 us5.datadoghq.com https://mcp.us5.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp EU1 datadoghq.eu https://mcp.datadoghq.eu/v1/mcp AP1 ap1.datadoghq.com https://mcp.ap1.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp AP2 ap2.datadoghq.com https://mcp.ap2.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp UK1 uk1.datadoghq.com https://mcp.uk1.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp US1-FED ddog-gov.com Not supported US2-FED us2.ddog-gov.com Not supported Toolsets The Datadog MCP Server supports toolsets , which allow you to use only the MCP tools you need, saving valuable context window space. To use a toolset, include the toolsets query parameter in the endpoint URL when connecting to the MCP Server ( remote authentication only). Use toolsets=all to enable all generally available toolsets (except for the chat toolset ) at once. Enabling all toolsets increases the number of tool definitions sent to your AI client, which consumes context window space. toolsets=all works best with clients that support tool search. Tools in Preview and the chat toolset are not included in toolsets=all . To use them, explicitly add the toolset to the toolsets parameter (for example, ?toolsets=all,apm,chat ). For example, based on your selected Datadog site ( ): Retrieve only the core tools (this is the default if toolsets is not specified): Retrieve only Synthetic Testing-related tools: ?toolsets=synthetics Retrieve core, Synthetic Testing, and Software Delivery tools: ?toolsets=core,synthetics,software-delivery Retrieve all generally available tools (except for the chat toolset ): ?toolsets=all For the Codex CLI, use the X-Datadog-MCP-Toolsets header described in the Codex setup instructions , not the query parameter described here. Omit specific tools Use the omit_tools query parameter to remove specific tools from the final tool list. Examples for your selected site ( ): Omit tools from the default set: ?omit_tools=search_datadog_logs,search_datadog_spans Select toolsets, then omit one tool: ?toolsets=core,software-delivery&omit_tools=search_datadog_incidents Start from all generally available toolsets, then omit write tools: ?toolsets=all&omit_tools=create_datadog_notebook,edit_datadog_notebook Provide tool names as a comma-separated list. When both parameters are present, the server resolves toolsets first and then removes matching tools in omit_tools . If omit_tools includes unknown tool names, the server warns and continues. Available toolsets These toolsets are generally available. See Datadog MCP Server Tools for a complete reference of available tools organized by toolset, with example prompts. core : The default toolset for logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, monitors, incidents, hosts, services, events, notebooks, and code execution. alerting : Tools for validating and creating monitors, searching monitor groups, retrieving monitor templates, analyzing monitor coverage, and searching SLOs. apm : Tools for APM , including checking service health, investigating errors and latency, finding optimization opportunities, and managing sampling and service remapping rules. Some tools in this toolset are in Preview and are available only when you request apm by name and have Preview access ( sign up ). See Datadog MCP Server Tools for details. audit-trail : Tools for Audit Trail , including searching and retrieving Audit Trail events and forming Audit Trail search queries. cases : Tools for Work Management , including creating, searching, updating, and commenting on work items (cases); managing projects; linking work items to each other and to Jira issues; managing attachments; and finding users to assign. Some tools in this toolset are in Preview and are available only when you request cases by name. Required permissions The Datadog MCP Server requires both user role permissions and organization-wide access . See the following sections for details. For a complete overview of MCP access controls, including how to restrict the actions an individual AI client can perform, see Access Control for MCP . User role permissions MCP Server tools require the following Datadog user role permissions : Permission Required for mcp_read Tools that read data from Datadog (for example, querying monitors, searching logs, retrieving dashboards) mcp_write Tools that create or modify resources in Datadog (for example, creating monitors, muting hosts) In addition to mcp_read or mcp_write , users need the standard Datadog permissions for the underlying resource. For example, using an MCP tool that reads monitors requires both mcp_read and the Monitors Read permission. See Datadog Role Permissions for the full list of resource-level permissions. Users with the Datadog Standard Role have both MCP Server permissions by default. If your organization uses custom roles , add the permissions manually: Go to Organization Settings > Roles as an administrator, and click the role you want to update. Click Edit Role (pencil icon). Under the permissions list, select the MCP Read and MCP Write checkboxes. Select any other resource-level permissions you need for the role. Click Save . Organization-wide access MCP Server tools also require global, organization-wide MCP access and write capabilities, which organization administrators manage in Organization Settings . Enable these settings to allow access to the Datadog MCP Server and its tools: Organization Setting Description MCP Access Enable to allow access to the Datadog MCP Server. When disabled, users cannot access any MCP functionality, regardless of individual role permissions. This allows organizations to completely opt out of the MCP Server. MCP Write Access Enable to allow access to MCP Server tools that create or modify resources, such as create_datadog_monitor . When disabled, the MCP Server hides write tools from all users, regardless of individual role permissions. See Troubleshooting for more information. Restrict network access To control which networks can connect to the Datadog MCP Server, enable the IP allowlist . This prevents users from connecting to the MCP Server from unapproved origins, even if they have the required permissions. Authentication For most users, OAuth 2.0 is the recommended authentication method, and your MCP client handles it during setup. Use one of the header-based methods below only when you cannot complete the OAuth flow, for example on a server or in a CI environment. OAuth 2.0 (recommended) Most clients complete the OAuth 2.0 flow automatically during setup. Select your client at the top of this page for instructions. With OAuth, you don’t manage long-lived credentials directly. For details, see the MCP authorization specification . Custom subdomains If your organization signs in through a custom subdomain, such as <SUBDOMAIN>.datadoghq.com , add the subdomain query parameter to the endpoint URL. The MCP client uses this value to send the OAuth flow directly to your subdomain. Without it, the flow starts on the default Datadog domain, so users already signed in on their subdomain are redirected and have to sign in again before they can be authorized. For example, based on your selected Datadog site ( ): ?subdomain=<SUBDOMAIN> To combine subdomain with toolsets or other query parameters, separate them with & : ?subdomain=<SUBDOMAIN>&toolsets=apm,llmobs Revoke OAuth access When you authorize an MCP client, Datadog creates a consent grant scoped to your user, that client, and the organization you selected during the OAuth flow. Revoking the grant invalidates the client’s credentials, and the client must complete the OAuth flow again to reconnect. Note : A client that already holds a valid access token can keep making requests until that token expires. Revoking prevents it from obtaining a new one. To revoke your own access for a client: In Datadog, navigate to Personal Settings > Authorized Apps . Find the MCP client you want to disconnect and hover over it to show a removal icon. Click the removal icon and from the modal, revoke the authorization. Repeat for each client and each organization you authorized from. Revoking an authorization has no effect on Personal Access Tokens, Service Access Tokens, or API and application keys. Delete or rotate those in their own management pages. Administrators can disable an AI client or remove specific scopes from it for the entire organization. To do this, use the Mobile and Third-Party Access page. See Restrict actions for a specific AI client . Personal or Service Access Token For header-based authentication, a Datadog Personal Access Token (PAT) or Service Access Token (SAT) is the preferred option. Pass the token as a bearer token in the Authorization header. No API key is required. For example, based on your selected Datadog site ( ): {
  "mcpServers": {
    "datadog": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": " ",
      "headers": {
          "Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN>"
      }
    }
  }
} Use a PAT for an individual user or a SAT for a service account . For scopes, token management, and other authentication methods, see the PAT and SAT documentation. API and application keys Alternatively, provide a Datadog API key and application key as DD_API_KEY and DD_APPLICATION_KEY HTTP headers: For example, based on your selected Datadog site ( ): {
  "mcpServers": {
    "datadog": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": " ",
      "headers": {
          "DD_API_KEY": "<YOUR_API_KEY>",
          "DD_APPLICATION_KEY": "<YOUR_APPLICATION_KEY>"
      }
    }
  }
} For security, use a scoped API key and application key from a service account that has only the required permissions. Note : An AI client’s OAuth application scopes do not apply to connections that use API and application keys or access tokens. These connections have the access of the key or token. Adding OAuth clients To allow-list a redirect URL, open MCP OAuth Redirect URLs in Organization Settings, enter the URL, and select Add URL . If you are a partner or vendor adding Datadog to an MCP directory for your AI agent platform, submit your interest through Datadog’s Technology Partner Signup . Test access to the MCP Server Install the MCP inspector , a developer tool for testing and debugging MCP servers. npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector In the inspector’s web UI, for Transport Type , select Streamable HTTP . For URL , enter the MCP Server endpoint for your regional Datadog site. For example, for : Click Connect , then go to Tools > List Tools . Check if the available tools appear. Troubleshooting Write tools are missing If your AI client does not list Datadog MCP Server tools that create or modify resources (such as create_datadog_monitor ), check the following: Organization write access : When MCP write capabilities are disabled for your organization, the MCP Server hides write tools from the tool list for all users, regardless of individual user role permissions. An organization administrator can enable MCP Write Access from Organization Settings . Role permissions : Confirm that your role includes the mcp_write permission and the permission for the underlying resource, such as Monitors Write for creating monitors. See Required permissions . Toolsets : Confirm that you enabled the toolset that contains the tool. If you don’t specify toolsets, only core tools are available. For example, create_datadog_monitor is in the alerting toolset. Preview toolsets are not included in toolsets=all , so request them by name. Omitted tools : Confirm that the tool is not listed in the omit_tools query parameter. OAuth application scopes : If an administrator removed a scope from your AI client, you cannot use that client for actions that need the scope. This applies even if your role includes the permission. See Restrict actions for a specific AI client . After you change any of these settings, refresh the tool list in your AI client. Reconnecting the client is a typical way to do this, but some AI clients provide other ways to refresh the tool list. Access Control for MCP Docs > Account Management > Access Control > Access Control for MCP The Datadog MCP Server lets AI agents and clients, such as Claude Code, Cursor, and ChatGPT, read and act on Datadog data on behalf of a signed-in user. You can control which users can access the MCP Server, whether they can write through it, and which actions each AI client can perform, even when the user can perform those actions elsewhere in Datadog. Datadog evaluates MCP access in layers. A request through the MCP Server succeeds only if every layer allows it: Layer Control Scope Default 1 MCP Access organization setting Entire organization On 2 MCP Write Access organization setting Entire organization Off 3 IP allowlist Entire organization Off 4 MCP Read and MCP Write role permissions Per role - Datadog Read Only role: MCP Read - Datadog Standard and Admin roles: MCP Read and MCP Write 5 OAuth application scopes Per AI client All requested scopes allowed 6 Standard Datadog access controls Per user, resource, and dataset Same as in the Datadog UI and API The MCP Server never grants a user more access than they already have in Datadog. Each layer can only narrow access further. Enable or disable the Datadog MCP Server The MCP Access organization setting controls whether anyone in your organization can use the Datadog MCP Server. It is enabled by default. When MCP Access is disabled, no user can access any MCP functionality, regardless of their role permissions. To change this setting, you must be an organization administrator. Navigate to Organization Settings > MCP . Toggle MCP Access on or off. Enable or disable MCP write access The MCP Write Access organization setting controls whether agents can create, modify, or delete resources through the MCP Server. It is disabled by default. When MCP Write Access is disabled, the MCP Server hides write tools from all users, regardless of their role permissions. Read tools remain available to users with the MCP Read permission. To change this setting, you must be an organization administrator. Navigate to Organization Settings > MCP . Toggle MCP Write Access on or off. Enabling MCP Write Access does not let every user write. Each user also needs the MCP Write permission and the standard write permission for the resource, such as Monitors Write . Restrict network access To control which networks can connect to the Datadog MCP Server, enable the IP allowlist . When the IP allowlist is enabled, users cannot connect to the MCP Server from IP addresses outside the allowlist, even if they have the required permissions. Control MCP access for specific users Use role permissions to give specific users different MCP access from the rest of your organization. To turn off MCP access or MCP write access for every user, use the organization settings instead. Two role permissions control MCP access: Permission Internal name Grants MCP Read mcp_read Use MCP tools that read data. MCP Write mcp_write Use MCP tools that create or modify resources. Requires MCP Write Access to be enabled for the organization. By default, the Datadog Read Only role has MCP Read , and the Datadog Standard and Admin roles have both MCP Read and MCP Write . To give specific users MCP access that differs from the managed roles, assign them a custom role . For example, to let a group of users write in Datadog but only read through the MCP Server, create a custom role that includes MCP Read but not MCP Write , and assign it to those users. Navigate to Organization Settings > Roles . Select a custom role, or click New Role to create one. Click Edit Role . Under MCP , select or clear MCP Read and MCP Write . Click Save . Restrict actions for a specific AI client Each AI client that connects to the MCP Server through OAuth, such as Claude Code, is registered as an OAuth application in your organization. Each application requests a set of scopes, which correspond to Datadog permissions. Use Application Scope Management to remove scopes from an AI client’s OAuth application. A removed scope blocks that action through the AI client, even if the user has permission to perform it elsewhere in Datadog. For example, a user with Dashboards Write can still edit dashboards in the Datadog UI, but cannot edit them through Claude Code if you remove the dashboards_write scope from the Claude Code OAuth application. Scope changes apply to every user in your organization who uses that AI client. Prerequisites You need the Datadog Admin role, or a role with both the Org Authorized Apps Read ( org_authorized_apps_read ) and Org Authorized Apps Write ( org_authorized_apps_write ) permissions. Manage scopes Navigate to Organization Settings > Mobile and Third-Party Access . Click the OAuth application for the AI client you want to restrict. Click the Scopes tab. Clear the Allowed checkbox for each scope you want to block. Clear Automatically allow new scopes so that scopes the AI client requests in the future are blocked until an administrator allows them. Click Save . Note : Removing a scope revokes existing authorizations that include that scope. Affected users must reauthorize the AI client to regain access with the remaining allowed scopes. Adding a scope does not add it to existing authorizations; users must reauthorize to receive it. Example: Allow agents to write only to Notebooks To let agents read data across Datadog but only write to Notebooks: Enable MCP Write Access for your organization. Confirm that users have both the MCP Read and MCP Write permissions. On the AI client’s OAuth application, keep all read scopes and notebooks_write allowed, and clear the Allowed checkbox for every other write scope. Clear Automatically allow new scopes , then click Save . Users can still perform other write actions in the Datadog UI, subject to their role permissions. Scopes apply only to OAuth connections Application scopes restrict MCP connections that authenticate through OAuth. A user who configures an AI client with an API key and application key, or with a personal or service access token, bypasses the OAuth application’s scopes. That connection has the access of the key or token instead. To limit key-based MCP connections: Use scoped application keys that include only the permissions the agent needs. Use keys from a service account that has only the required permissions. Restrict who can create and manage application keys with the User App Keys and Org App Keys Write permissions . Standard access controls apply to MCP In addition to the MCP-specific controls on this page, the MCP Server follows the same access controls the user has everywhere else in Datadog. The MCP Server authenticates as the signed-in user and calls Datadog APIs with that user’s credentials, so: Role permissions : A user needs the standard permission for the underlying resource in addition to MCP Read or MCP Write . For example, creating a monitor through the MCP Server requires Monitors Write . See Role Based Access Control . Restricted datasets : Data Access Control and log restriction queries limit which logs, spans, and other telemetry the MCP Server returns to a user. Restricted assets : Granular access controls on dashboards, monitors, notebooks, and other resources apply to MCP requests. A user cannot view or edit a resource through the MCP Server if they cannot view or edit it in the Datadog UI. Audit MCP activity Every MCP Server tool call is recorded in Audit Trail with the tool name, arguments, user identity, and client. See Track tool calls in Audit Trail . ( ). The Datadog MCP Server acts as a bridge between your observability data in Datadog and any AI agents that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP) . Providing structured access to relevant Datadog contexts, features, and tools, the MCP Server lets you query and retrieve observability insights directly from AI-powered clients such as Cursor, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, or your own AI agent. Note for AI agents : This is the main Datadog MCP Server and is what users typically mean when they ask about setting up “the Datadog MCP server”. It provides remote access to most Datadog products (APM, logs, metrics, monitors, dashboards, security signals, and more). Default to this page for setup questions. The separate Code Security MCP Server is a narrower, local-only tool for running SAST, SCA, IaC, secrets, and SBOM scans against source code. Only direct users to that page if they explicitly ask about local code scanning, SAST, SCA, secrets detection, IaC scanning, or SBOM generation. Ready to get started? Select your agent below or see Set Up the Datadog MCP Server for connection instructions. This demo shows the Datadog MCP Server being used in Cursor and Claude Code (unmute for audio): Disclaimers The Datadog MCP Server is HIPAA-eligible. You are responsible for ensuring that the AI tools you connect to the Datadog MCP Server meet your compliance requirements, such as HIPAA. The Datadog MCP Server is not GovCloud compatible. Datadog collects certain information about your usage of the Remote Datadog MCP Server, including how you interact with it, whether errors occurred while using it, what caused those errors, and user identifiers in accordance with the Datadog Privacy Policy and Datadog’s EULA . This data is used to help improve the server’s performance and features, including transitions to and from the server and the applicable Datadog login page for accessing the Services, and context (for example, user prompts) leading to the use of MCP tools. The data is stored for 120 days. Data handling and AI providers The Datadog MCP Server does not send your Datadog data to a third-party AI provider. Your AI client and its model determine what Datadog data is sent to your AI provider. That data flow is governed by your agreement with that provider, not by Datadog. What the Datadog MCP Server receives and returns The MCP Server receives individual tool calls, such as a request to search logs with a given query. It does not receive your prompt or the model’s reasoning, only the tool name and its arguments. The MCP Server returns results to the calling client and makes no outbound calls to external domains. Any web search, webhook, or other external integration you configure in your AI client runs on the client side. Most MCP Server tools, such as search_datadog_logs , query Datadog backends directly with no AI model involved. A small number of tools do use AI models hosted by Datadog’s AI providers. Examples include tools that perform semantic search or build a query from a natural language description. To disable generative AI providers for your entire organization, contact Datadog support . Restrict which data the Datadog MCP Server can access The MCP Server forwards the authenticated user’s own credentials to Datadog APIs. Your existing access controls apply exactly as they do for direct API or UI access. The MCP Server cannot grant a user access beyond what that user already has. It cannot reach resources that are not visible to that user in the Datadog UI. Because your AI client controls what it sends to its model provider, limiting what a provider can receive means limiting what the MCP Server returns. To scope the data an MCP Server user can retrieve, use: Role-based access control (RBAC) to grant permissions by role. Data Access Control to restrict which users can read sensitive data, such as logs or APM spans. Log restriction queries to limit a role’s log access to the subset of logs matching a query. Write operations require the corresponding permission, such as monitors_write , and the MCP Server checks it on each tool call. A read-only user’s call to a write-enabled tool is rejected. Administrators can also turn off the MCP Server or its write tools for the entire organization. They can restrict which actions each AI client can perform, even when a user can perform those actions elsewhere in Datadog. See Access Control for MCP . Fair-use rate limits The MCP Server has a fair-use burst limit of 50 tool calls per 10 seconds. There is no monthly limit on tool calls. This limit is subject to change , and Datadog can raise it if your use case requires more. Contact Datadog support for requests or questions. Monitoring the Datadog MCP Server tool calls You can track Datadog MCP Server usage for your organization using Datadog metrics and Audit Trail. All tool calls are recorded in the Datadog Audit Trail with metadata identifying them as MCP actions, including the tool name, arguments, user identity, and the MCP client used. See Track tool calls in Audit Trail for more information. Datadog also emits two standard metrics that you can use to monitor MCP Server activity: datadog.mcp.session.starts : Emitted on each session initialization. datadog.mcp.tool.usage : A distribution metric emitted on each tool call. Both metrics are tagged with attributes such as user_id , user_email , client (the MCP client name, such as claude or cursor ), and tool_name . Because datadog.mcp.tool.usage is a distribution metric, use count (not sum ) with .as_count() to get the number of tool calls. For example, to query the total number of tool calls grouped by user email: count : datadog . mcp . tool . usage { * } by { user_email } . as_count () Available tools See Datadog MCP Server Tools for a complete reference of available tools organized by toolset, with example prompts. To enable specific toolsets, see Set Up the Datadog MCP Server for instructions. Context efficiency The Datadog MCP Server is optimized to provide responses in a way that AI agents get relevant context without being overloaded with unnecessary information. For example: Responses are truncated based on the estimated length of responses each tool provides. The tools respond to AI agents with instructions on how to request more information if the response was truncated. Most tools have a max_tokens parameter that enables AI agents to request less or more information. You can limit available tools at connection time with toolsets and omit_tools . See Set Up the Datadog MCP Server . Track tool calls in Audit Trail You can view information about calls made by MCP Server tools in Datadog’s Audit Trail . The API uses resource-oriented URLs to call the API, uses status codes to indicate the success or failure of requests, returns JSON from all requests, and uses standard HTTP response codes. Use the Datadog API to access the Datadog platform programmatically. Getting started Authenticate to the API with an API key using the header DD-API-KEY . For some endpoints, you also need an Application key , which uses the header DD-APPLICATION-KEY . To try out the API Note : To authenticate to the Datadog API through Postman, add your Datadog API and Application key values to the Collection variables of the Datadog API collection. Using the API is a guide to the endpoints. Notes : Add your API and application key values to the Variables tab of the Datadog API Collection. cURL code examples assume usage of BASH and GNU coreutils. On macOS, you can install coreutils with the Homebrew package manager : brew install coreutils Client libraries By default, the Datadog API Docs show examples in cURL. Select one of our official client libraries languages in each endpoint to see code examples from that library. To install each library: Java Python [legacy] Python Ruby [legacy] Ruby Go TypeScript Rust Installation Maven - Add this dependency to your project's POM: Copy <dependency> <groupId> com.datadoghq </groupId> <artifactId> datadog-api-client </artifactId> <version> 2.62.0 </version> <scope> compile </scope> </dependency> Gradle - Add this dependency to your project's build file: Copy compile "com.datadoghq:datadog-api-client:2.62.0" Usage Copy import com.datadog.api.client.ApiClient; import com.datadog.api.client.ApiException; import com.datadog.api.client.Configuration; import com.datadog.api.<VERSION>.client.api.*; import com.datadog.api.<VERSION>.client.model.*; Note : Replace <VERSION> with v1 or v2, depending on which endpoints you want to use. Examples Maven pom.xml for running examples: Copy <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example </groupId> <artifactId> example </artifactId> <version> 1 </version> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.datadoghq </groupId> <artifactId> datadog-api-client </artifactId> <version> 2.62.0 </version> <scope> compile </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> Make sure that CLASSPATH variable contains all dependencies. Copy export CLASSPATH=$(mvn -q exec:exec -Dexec.executable=echo -Dexec.args="%classpath" ) Gradle build.gradle for running examples: Copy plugins { id 'java' id 'application' } repositories { jcenter() } dependencies { implementation 'com.datadoghq:datadog-api-client:2.62.0' } application { mainClassName = 'Example.java' } Execute example by running gradle run command. Installation Copy pip install datadog Usage Copy import datadog Installation Copy pip3 install datadog-api-client Usage Copy import datadog_api_client Installation Copy gem install dogapi Usage Copy require 'dogapi' Installation Copy gem install datadog_api_client -v 2.61.0 Usage Copy require 'datadog_api_client' Installation Copy go mod init main && go get github.com/DataDog/datadog-api-client-go/v2/api/datadog Usage Copy import ( "github.com/DataDog/datadog-api-client-go/v2/api/datadog" "github.com/DataDog/datadog-api-client-go/v2/api/datadog<VERSION>" ) Note : Replace <VERSION> with V1 or V2 , depending on which endpoints you want to use. Installation The package is under @datadog/datadog-api-client and can be installed through NPM or Yarn: Copy # NPM npm install @datadog/datadog-api-client # Yarn yarn add @datadog/datadog-api-client Usage Copy import { <VERSION> } from 'datadog-api-client' ; Note : Replace <VERSION> with v1 or v2, depending on which endpoints you want to use. Installation Run cargo add datadog-api-client , or add the following to Cargo.toml under [dependencies] : Copy datadog-api-client = "0" Usage Try the following snippet to validate your Datadog API key: Copy use datadog_api_client::datadog:: Configuration ; use datadog_api_client::datadogV1::api_authentication:: AuthenticationAPI ; #[tokio::main] async fn main() { let configuration = Configuration ::new(); let api = AuthenticationAPI ::with_config(configuration); let resp = api.validate(). await ; if let Ok (value) = resp { println!( " { :#? } " , value); } else { println!( " { :#? } " , resp.unwrap_err()); } } Or check out the libraries directly: Trying to get started with the application instead?
